chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 361 to 370, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade of direct address (முன்னிலைப் பத்து): each poem speaks to someone face to face, the man to the girl whose beauty strikes him and to a mango shoot like her, the friend to the man who comes by night, who would hurry away, who has been gossiped about, and to the mother asking why the girl is pale, all set among the kongu, paathiri and silk-cotton of the dry season and the hunters of the waste.

361.reading: The man tells the simple girl who wears a garland strung from summer paathiri flowers heaped on the wide shining sand of a high-banked forest stream that her breasts strike harder than her eyes, and her broad soft shoulders harder than her breasts.
361.nuance: The climb runs against the usual order of the love poems, where the eyes are the weapon: here each part of her is fiercer (கதவ) than the last, so the praise turns into a mock complaint of being attacked, while the paathiri garland shows her at ease in the waste.

thinai_evidence.note: a forest stream in summer with paathiri in flower is the waste in its season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the man addresses the girl directly (மடவரல் மகளே); the summer stream and the garland she has made on the way point to the couple on the road of elopement, as in Akananuru 99, though the poem does not say so

362.reading: The speaker asks the man with the flower-garlanded chest how he came in the night, when the dark pressed in, by the forked paths hard to walk and strewn with stone cairns, giving no thought to the deadly hatred of the small-eyed elephant, driven by a heart bent on kindness.
362.nuance: The cairns (பதுக்கை) are the waste's graves of travellers, so the kurinji visit by night is set on a paalai road; the line அருள்புரி நெஞ்சம் turns the reproach into praise, since what drove him across it was kindness, not mere desire.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's night journey to the tryst and the fear it raises is the kurinji situation, though the road is the waste's

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend (or the girl herself) questions the man who has come by night; the decade's direct address makes the complaint of the dangerous road a question put to his face

363.reading: The man tells the sister of the killing Eyinar, who carry bows with arrows and wear red-dyed cloth, that she takes the pale spots on her breasts for mere freckling, while his stricken heart takes them for a goddess that strikes.
363.nuance: The poem turns on a rhyme, சுணங்கு against அணங்கு: the same mark is a blemish of the skin to her and a dread power to him, and the killing trade of her brothers (கொலைவல் எயினர்) stands behind the girl, so the danger he feels is doubled.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl is of the bow-carrying hunters of the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the man speaks to the girl (நின், நீயே) about his own heart

364.reading: The speaker asks the young man of the white spear not to hurry until she has told the young Eyitri, sister of the Eyinar who live on porcupine, how things stand and has pleaded with her.
364.nuance: The -உம் of எயிற்றிக்கும் (to the Eyitri too) suggests the youth has already been told and the girl has not, so the friend stands between his haste and the girl's consent; இளமா may be a young doe or a young mango, either a likeness of the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunters of the waste and the youth of the paalai road

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend asks the youth (விடலை) to wait while she speaks to the girl; the occasion is most likely the plan to leave together, which she must first put to the girl

365.reading: The man asks a tender mango shoot what penance it did to have such desirable beauty, like the lovely-toothed Eyitri who drives off the birds that come at the fat meat her brothers brought home after killing deer from the herd.
365.nuance: The comparison is reversed: the shoot is praised for being like the girl, not the girl for being like the shoot, so the question 'what penance did you do?' measures her beauty as a thing a plant must earn.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl of the hunters of the waste, among their kill

comparisons.tenor: the mango shoot's colour and beauty

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the man addresses a mango shoot (மாஇன் தளிரே), comparing it with the girl

366.reading: The friend tells the mother that if she, with reddened eyes, keeps pressing for no purpose, saying the girl has grown very pale, nothing will come of it: the pallor is because the kongu with its tender-leaved clusters has come into flower.
366.nuance: The answer hides and reveals at once: the flowering kongu is the season the man would have named for his coming, so the friend's seasonal excuse is also a hint to the mother that the pallor has a man behind it.

thinai_evidence.note: the kongu's flowering in the dry season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend answers the mother's questioning with the formula of Akananuru 48 (அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை); whether the hearer is the mother or the foster mother is not fixed

367.reading: The friend tells the mother that the girl's life is now joined to the name of the man who came near with his chariot by the summer forest stream strewn with spread blossoms, wearing the gold-like fresh flowers of the rough-barked kongu set apart with the open clusters of vengai.
367.nuance: பேரொடு புணர்ந்தன்று is stronger than a story of meeting: her life is united not with the man but with his name, as if already married to it, and that is the friend's whole case to the mother.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer forest stream fixes the waste in its season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend tells the mother (அன்னை) that the girl belongs to the man

368.reading: The speaker asks the lord to share with them the pleasure of the cool spell of summer, when the many spent blossoms of the fire-flowered silk-cotton stripe the dappled shade of the puffed-flowered pungu, if he wishes her of the soft dark hair not to be ruined.
368.nuance: The dissuasion makes no argument against the journey; it offers a season too sweet to leave, and only the last line, அழிவிலள் எனினே, shows the threat inside the invitation.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer season of the waste, with its silk-cotton in flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend tries to hold back the man from a journey by inviting him to the season's pleasure, with the girl's ruin as the price of his going

369.reading: The speaker tells the man that the gossip, louder than the cry of the great koel of the season that lives on the long kuravam branch, says that yesterday he made a tryst with a woman whose smile is a row of sprouts, in the fragrant grove thick with rich flowers where bees swarm.
369.nuance: கௌவை means both a loud cry and public talk, so the koel's seasonal call and the town's gossip are measured on one scale, and the gossip wins; a tryst only one day old (நெருநல்) is already louder than the season.

thinai_evidence.note: the kuravam and the koel of early summer

comparisons.tenor: the town's gossip about the tryst

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend tells the man that his tryst is known; the woman of the tryst may be the girl herself, which makes this a warning that urges marriage, or another woman, which makes it a reproach

370.reading: The speaker asks the man to tell her, and not hide it, who the woman is that he longs for and lives for, while the great swarm of dark-winged bees crowds the cool fragrant garland of rich-branched kongu.
370.nuance: The bee-swarmed garland can be the man's gift or the woman's ornament; either way the bees give away where it has been, and the friend's 'do not hide it from us' presses him to own the love openly.

thinai_evidence.note: the kongu garland of the dry season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (முன்னிலைப் பத்து, poems of direct address); the friend asks the man, who comes with a kongu garland swarmed by bees, who the woman is, as if she did not know; the question could also be a wife's suspicion

links.note: In Akananuru 99 the man leading the eloped girl through the waste likens the opening kongu buds to women's jewelled breasts and points to paathiri petals on the path; in Ainkurunuru 361 the girl wears a paathiri garland by the summer stream and her breasts and shoulders strike him harder than her eyes.
links.teaches: Akananuru 99 makes the waste's flowers stand for her body to coax her onward, while 361 has her wearing those same flowers and her body outdoing them, so the eloping man's praise moves from comparing the land to her to letting her eclipse it.

links.note: Kural 1085 finds death, the eye and the doe all in the young woman's look; Ainkurunuru 361 grants the eyes are fierce, then ranks her breasts fiercer and her shoulders fiercer still.
links.teaches: The Kural's chapter on the first sight puts all the deadliness in the look, and the Ainkurunuru poet answers that the eyes are only the first and mildest weapon, which shows the old akam poets could treat the same stricken lover as half joking where the couplet keeps him grave.

links.note: In Natrinai 144 the girl, with the man overhearing, says her heart frets now that she knows he comes alone by night over the forked paths (கவலை) where the tigress prowls; in Ainkurunuru 362 the same fear of the forked night path (கவலை) and its elephant is put to the man's face.
links.teaches: The overheard complaint of Natrinai 144 and the open question of 362 make the same plea, stop coming by night, in two registers, and holding them together shows that Ainkurunuru's direct-address decade turns the indirect device of the overhearer into plain speech without changing the situation.

links.note: Kural 1081: on first sight the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels; Ainkurunuru 363: the man tells the hunters' sister that what she calls freckles (சுணங்கு) his stricken heart calls a goddess (அணங்கு).
links.teaches: Where the couplet leaves the goddess as one of three guesses about the whole woman, 363 pins the striking power on one small mark she herself thinks a blemish, so the pair shows the anangu is not in her but in the gap between how she sees herself and how he is struck.

links.note: Both open with the friend's formula to the mother, அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை, answering her question why the girl has grown pale (பசந்தனள்); in Akananuru 48 the friend tells the whole story of the hunter who came asking after a tiger, in 366 she answers only that the kongu has flowered.
links.teaches: The shared formula shows these are two answers to one stock question: Akananuru 48 discloses the love by a full story and leaves the wise to infer the rest, while 366 compresses the same disclosure into one seasonal sign, so the reader learns how far the friend's hint could be shortened and still be understood.

links.note: In Akananuru 317 the man had promised to come back in the spring when the kongu and kuravam flower and the koel calls, and his arrival ends a pallor the mother had noticed; in Ainkurunuru 366 the friend tells the mother the girl's pallor is because the kongu has flowered.
links.teaches: Read through 317, the friend's excuse in 366 is no excuse at all: the kongu's flowering is the season a man promises to return by, so pointing the mother to the tree points her to an absent lover, and the pair shows a seasonal sign doing the work of a confession.

links.note: In Akananuru 48 the friend tells the foster mother of a youth with a flower garland and a chariot who stopped by the vengai slope and gazed at the girl; in Ainkurunuru 367 the friend tells the mother of the man who came near with his chariot wearing kongu and vengai flowers, and says the girl's life is joined to his name.
links.teaches: The same disclosure scene, chariot, flowered youth and vengai included, ends in Akananuru 48 with an inference left to the mother and in 367 with a flat verdict that the girl is already bound to him, which shows the friend's revelation could be pitched as a hint or as a fait accompli.

links.note: In Kural 1151 the friend tells the departing man to promise a quick return only to those who will still be alive; in Ainkurunuru 368 the friend invites him to stay and enjoy the cool summer with them if the girl is not to be ruined.
links.teaches: Both hold the girl's life against the journey, but the couplet does it by refusing his comfort and 368 by tempting him with the season's pleasure, so together they show the two strategies of the friend who would stop a departure, the bitter and the sweet, around the same threat.

links.note: In Kural 1146 the woman says she saw him on one day only and the gossip has spread like the snake seizing the moon; in Ainkurunuru 369 the friend tells the man that his tryst of yesterday (நெருநல்) is already louder in the town's mouth than the seasonal koel.
links.teaches: Both measure a single meeting against a public noise, the eclipse in the couplet and the koel's cry in 369, and holding them together shows the alar topic's fixed shape: the smaller and more recent the secret, the larger the natural event the gossip is said to outdo.

source_issues.issue: The colophon has no thurai for any poem of this decade; speakers in thurai_akam are inferred from the poems.
Line 5 was repaired from the sangamtamil.com reading (முறியிணர்க் கோங்கம்); the sense of பயந்த மாறே (because the kongu bore flowers) carries the poem, so it is marked uncertain.
